planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late fall or late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; SweeTango needs a compatible pollinator such as another mid-season apple and full sun for best fruit quality.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby, since apples are not reliably self-fertile. Developed by the University of Minnesota from a cross of Honeycrisp and the earlier-ripening Zestar!, SweeTango combines Honeycrisp's signature explosive crunch and juiciness with a sweeter, more complex, slightly spicy flavor and a harvest window about three weeks ahead of its famous parent. The tree bears at a younger age and more heavily than Honeycrisp, though the fruit is prone to bitter pit and benefits from consistent watering and calcium availability during fruit development. Because it is a managed variety, most trees are sold under license through Next Big Thing Growers, but home gardeners can still plant and grow it for personal use; thin fruit to one per cluster for the best size and to reduce biennial bearing.

common_name: Ozark Gold Apple (Early-Season Golden Delicious-Type Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late fall or late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; Ozark Gold ripens several weeks ahead of Golden Delicious and needs a compatible early- to mid-season pollinator.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Released by the University of Missouri as an early-ripening improvement on Golden Delicious, Ozark Gold produces medium to large, smooth, yellow-gold fruit with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flesh, ready for picking in mid to late summer well ahead of its parent. Its early ripening and heat tolerance have made it a long-standing favorite for southern and midwestern home orchards where summer heat can push standard Golden Delicious to ripen unevenly. Like other Golden Delicious types, the thin skin bruises easily, so handle fruit gently at harvest, and thin clusters to one apple each in late spring to improve size and reduce biennial bearing.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late fall or late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; Winecrisp carries genetic resistance to apple scab, cutting down significantly on the fungicide sprays other apples need.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Winecrisp was bred through the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistance breeding program and carries genetic resistance to apple scab along with good resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it a strong choice for low-spray home orchards. Fruit is medium-sized with dark red skin over crisp, dense, wine-tinted flesh with a tangy-sweet flavor that improves in storage, and the tree stores exceptionally well into winter. Harvest in mid to late fall once background color shifts from green to yellow, and thin fruit clusters to one apple each in late spring to encourage consistent annual bearing and better fruit size.

common_name: Meteor Tart Cherry (Cold-Hardy Compact Pie Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late fall or late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; Meteor is self-fertile and does not need a pollinator, and its compact size and extreme cold hardiness make it a good option for northern gardens.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this self-fertile sour cherry needs no second tree to set fruit. Released by the University of Minnesota, Meteor is a naturally dwarf, extremely cold-hardy tart cherry bred to survive winters too harsh for Montmorency, the standard commercial pie cherry, while producing similar bright red, juicy, tart fruit for pies, preserves, and juice. Its compact, rounded habit tops out well below standard sweet cherry trees, making it easier to net against birds and to harvest without a ladder. Fruit ripens in a concentrated window in midsummer; harvest by cutting or gently pulling clusters, and net the tree as fruit colors up since birds find it just as appealing as gardeners do.

common_name: Georgia Belle Peach (Classic Southern White Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late fall or late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; Georgia Belle is self-fertile and has a moderate chill requirement (around 850 hours), suiting it to the mid-South more than the Deep Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this self-fertile heirloom needs no second tree to set fruit. A 19th-century Georgia heirloom still prized today, Georgia Belle bears large, mostly white-fleshed freestone fruit blushed with red over a creamy background, with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor that many old-time Southern gardeners consider unmatched by modern yellow-fleshed commercial peaches. The tree ripens in mid to late summer and bears reliably where its moderate chill requirement is met, though the soft, thin-skinned fruit bruises easily and does not ship well, which is part of why it remains mostly a dooryard and farmstand variety rather than a supermarket peach. Thin fruit to one per 6-8 inches of branch in late spring to improve size, and pick when the background color turns from green to creamy white or yellow and the fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure.
